# Welcome to the Keepance demo

You are inside a pretend professional workspace, running entirely in your browser. Everything you see is a real Keepance surface, just pre-seeded so you can poke around without setting anything up.

## What to try

1. Open `Notes/Customer Discovery - Acme Co Interview.md` and read a real-feeling interview transcript.
2. Open `Chats/Naming the product.aichat` and watch a saved AI conversation play back.
3. Browse the `Templates/` folder. Each file is one of the included workflow templates that ship with Keepance.
4. Open the AI sidebar and ask a question. The demo uses a shared, rate-limited Anthropic key.
5. Hit a limit? Paste your own Anthropic key into the BYOK input for unlimited use, or download the desktop app.

Nothing here is saved to a server. Refreshing the page brings the workspace back to its starting state.

# Customer Discovery: Acme Co Interview

**Date:** 2026-04-22
**Interviewee:** Sarah Chen, Head of Operations
**Duration:** 38 minutes

## Background

Sarah runs ops at a 22-person B2B logistics startup. They use a mix of Notion, Slack, and a homegrown Airtable thing for project tracking.

## Pain points she named

- "Every project doc starts in Notion, then important parts get pasted into Slack, then somebody asks a question and we lose the thread."
- Three different people are writing the same kind of weekly update from scratch every Friday.
- New hires take two weeks to find anything because nothing is filed consistently.

## Quotes I want to remember

> "I don't need another tool. I need the tools I have to stop fighting me."

> "If I could just talk to my notes, I'd be 30 percent faster."

## Open questions

- Is the bottleneck the search, the structure, or the writing?
- Would she pay $49 once for something that fixed this, or does it have to be a SaaS?
- Where do her engineers fit? She kept saying "my team" without distinguishing roles.

## Next step

Follow up with the same questions to two more ops leads at similar-stage companies. Look for the same three patterns.

# Pricing experiments

Keeping a running list of pricing pages I have looked at so I don't keep relearning the same lessons.

## What I am leaning toward

One-time purchase, three tiers: Free, Pro, Lifetime. No subscription. The pitch is "buy it once, own it forever."

## What I have seen work for similar tools

- **Obsidian:** free for personal, $50/yr for sync, $25 one-time for Catalyst supporter. Sync is genuinely the only paid feature.
- **Tana:** subscription only, premium features behind a paywall. Hard to justify for a single founder.
- **Reflect:** $10/mo subscription, no free tier. Users churn.
- **Logseq:** free, donation model. Survives but does not grow.

## Hypothesis

Professionals tolerate a one-time charge better than a subscription, even if the subscription is cheaper over a year. Anchor: Sublime Text, BBEdit, Things.

## Current pricing

$49 Personal / $129 Professional (includes one profession pack) / $399 Practice (up to 5 seats). Sold via LemonSqueezy. Charter pricing: $89 for first 100 Professional buyers per profession pack.

# Roadmap Q3 2026

## Themes

- Onboarding: get a new user to their first useful AI chat in under three minutes.
- Templates: fill out the template library so the empty-state never feels empty.
- Performance: the editor must stay snappy with a 5,000-file workspace.

## Locked in

- v1.5 with auto-updater (shipped)
- Document suite: docx, xlsx, pptx, pdf rendering (shipped)
- Web demo at keepance.com/try (in flight, this is what you are looking at)

## Maybe

- Mobile read-only viewer (research first, no commitment)
- Plugin system (defer to v2.5 at the earliest)

## Won't do this quarter

- Real-time collab
- Cloud sync
- Server-side anything

# Why I picked local-first

Notes for a blog post.

## The 30-second version

My data lives on my machine. My API keys live in my OS keychain. AI requests go from my computer to the model provider, never via Keepance's servers. If Keepance the company disappears tomorrow, my files are still there as plain Markdown.

## Why this matters now

Every AI workspace tool is racing to put my data on their servers so they can train on it, sell ads against it, or upsell me into their cloud tier. Local-first is a deliberate choice not to do that.

## The tradeoffs I am accepting

- No real-time collab. (I am building for attorneys, CPAs, and consultants, who do not need it.)
- No magic cross-device sync. (You can use iCloud, Dropbox, Syncthing, or Git for that.)
- I cannot show you a usage dashboard, because I do not see your usage.

## What I get back

- A pricing model where I sell the app once, not a subscription to my servers.
- Privacy claims I can actually back up.
- A product that keeps working when the internet is down.

# Template: New Business Kickoff

**What it does:** Interviews you about your business idea, then generates three documents: a Vision document, a PRD, and a Lean Canvas.

## Interview questions

1. What problem are you solving?
2. What is your solution?
3. Who is your target customer?
4. What makes you unique?
5. How will you reach customers?
6. How will you make money?
7. Who are your competitors?
8. What stage is your business?

## Outputs

- `VISION.md` — executive summary, problem statement, solution overview, target market, vision statement, success metrics.
- `PRD.md` — overview, goals, user stories, requirements, success criteria, open questions.
- `LEAN_CANVAS.md` — the standard nine-section lean canvas.

In the desktop app, this workflow runs against your chosen AI provider with full read/write access to your workspace.

# Template: Customer Persona

**What it does:** Walks you through defining your ideal customer profile, then writes a persona document you can share with anyone on your team or pin to the wall.

## Interview questions

1. What does your product or service do?
2. Describe your best customers (or ideal customers if pre-launch).
3. What problems do your customers face?
4. What does success look like for them?
5. Where do they spend time online?
6. What other tools do they use?
7. What objections will they have about your product?

## Output

- `PERSONA.md` — name, role, demographics, daily pains, what success looks like, channels to reach them, common objections, the perfect pitch.

# Template: MVP Scope

**What it does:** Helps you cut your product idea down to the smallest thing you can actually ship. Outputs a clear scope document plus a list of what you are explicitly not building.

## Interview questions

1. What is the one job your MVP must do?
2. Who is the single user you are building this for?
3. What is the one outcome they are trying to achieve?
4. What is the smallest set of features that delivers that outcome?
5. What are you tempted to build that you should not?
6. How will you know it worked?

## Output

- `MVP_SCOPE.md` — the core job, the user, the outcome, the in-scope feature list, the explicit non-goals, the success metric.

# Template: Competitor Analysis

**What it does:** Builds a side-by-side comparison of your product against three to five competitors, plus a short narrative about where you win.

## Interview questions

1. Who are your top three to five competitors?
2. What are they known for?
3. Where do they fall short?
4. Where do you win?
5. What is the one thing you do that none of them do?

## Output

- `COMPETITORS.md` — comparison table (features, pricing, target user, strengths, weaknesses), then a narrative of your differentiated position.

# Template: Pricing Strategy

**What it does:** Walks you through the standard SaaS pricing decisions (tier count, anchor price, free tier, billing frequency) and outputs a pricing page draft.

## Interview questions

1. What is your business model? (subscription, one-time, usage-based)
2. What does your most direct competitor charge?
3. What is the smallest amount of value a customer gets in their first month?
4. Do you want a free tier? Why?
5. What is your most expensive customer worth to you?

## Output

- `PRICING.md` — recommended tier structure, suggested prices, free tier definition, the FAQ paragraphs you will need on the pricing page.

# Template: Pitch Deck

**What it does:** Produces the text content for the standard YC-style ten-slide investor deck. You take this into Figma or Keynote to design.

## Interview questions

1. What is your company name and tagline?
2. What problem are you solving?
3. What is your solution?
4. How big is the market?
5. What is your traction?
6. How do you make money?
7. Who is on your team?
8. How much are you raising?

## Output

- `PITCH_DECK.md` — ten slides with title and body copy: title, problem, solution, market, product, traction, business model, team, ask, vision.

# Template: Landing Page

**What it does:** Writes the copy for a one-page marketing site, then suggests three headline variants you can A/B test.

## Interview questions

1. Who is the primary visitor?
2. What single action do you want them to take?
3. What proof do you have that the product works?
4. What objection will they have?
5. What does your product NOT do that they might assume?

## Output

- `LANDING_PAGE.md` — hero headline, subhead, three feature blocks with copy, social proof section, FAQ, CTA. Plus three alternate headlines.

# Template: Go-to-Market Plan

**What it does:** Helps you decide where to spend your launch energy. Outputs a single-channel-first plan rather than a sprawling spray-and-pray.

## Interview questions

1. Where does your customer already hang out?
2. What is your single best channel for the first 100 customers?
3. What is your second best?
4. What launch moments do you have access to? (PH, HN, newsletters)
5. What does week one of the launch look like?

## Output

- `GTM.md` — primary channel deep dive, secondary channel notes, launch week timeline, week-two-and-beyond plan, the assets you need to make.

# Template: User Interviews

**What it does:** Generates a focused interview script for the customer segment you are trying to validate, plus a follow-up plan.

## Interview questions

1. Who are you trying to learn about?
2. What is the single biggest assumption you want to test?
3. How many people are you trying to talk to?
4. What does success look like for the interview round?

## Output

- `INTERVIEW_SCRIPT.md` — opening, eight to twelve open-ended questions, follow-up prompts, closing, plus a debrief template you fill in after each call.

# Template: Financial Model

**What it does:** Walks you through a 12-month projection for a software business. Outputs a Markdown table you can import into a spreadsheet.

## Interview questions

1. What is your pricing?
2. How many customers do you expect to acquire in months 1, 6, and 12?
3. What is your fixed monthly cost?
4. What is your variable cost per customer?
5. What growth rate are you assuming?

## Output

- `FINANCIAL_MODEL.md` — month-by-month revenue, costs, gross margin, cash position. Plus an assumptions section so future-you remembers what you guessed.

# Template: Investor Update

**What it does:** Drafts the monthly update email investors actually want to read. Short, structured, no fluff.

## Interview questions

1. What was the single biggest win this month?
2. What was the single biggest blocker?
3. What are the three numbers that matter? (MRR, customers, churn)
4. What do you need help with?
5. What is the one ask of the reader?

## Output

- `INVESTOR_UPDATE.md` — opening line, three numbers, wins, blockers, ask, signoff. Designed to fit in a phone screen.

# Template: Weekly Review

**What it does:** A reflection prompt at the end of each week. Generates a short journal entry plus three concrete things to do differently next week.

## Interview questions

1. What did you ship this week?
2. What did you learn?
3. What did you start but not finish?
4. What surprised you?
5. What will you do differently next week?

## Output

- `Weekly Reviews/<date>.md` — a dated journal entry with the answers above, plus a small Next Week section with three bullets you can copy into your task list.
